verbs.text: Creaked and groaned in the gale

sentences.text: Slender, silver birches swayed in the faintest breeze, their leaves trembling like coins.
Shafts of dappled, golden light slanted through the canopy and pooled among the ferns.
Ancient, moss-clad oaks towered above the path, older than the village, older perhaps than its name.
Gnarled, contorted boughs loomed out of the mist like the arms of drowning men.
Sodden, decaying leaves carpeted the forest floor and released a rich, loamy scent with every step.
Dense, thorny undergrowth clawed at his sleeves, as though the wood itself were reluctant to let him pass.
Overhead, the thick, interlaced canopy shut out the sky and turned noon into a green dusk.
The great trunks creaked and groaned in the gale, and somewhere deep in the wood a bough splintered with a crack like a rifle shot.
Bare branches thrashed against the sky as the storm tore through the treetops.
A faint, overgrown trail wound between the trunks before losing itself in bracken.
Squirrels darted from bough to bough, sending down a rain of twigs and bark.
Small birds flitted through the undergrowth, and the whole wood rang with their chatter.
A twig snapped beneath his foot, and the silence that followed seemed to listen.
As the light failed, long, brooding shadows crept across the clearing towards them.
One by one, the russet leaves spiralled slowly to the ground.
The cry of a single crow echoed through the trees of the bare, skeletal woodland.
Pale, feathery lichen clung to the bark of every trunk, a sign of clean air and great age.
They rested in a secluded, sunlit glade, on a cushion of deep, springy moss.
Verdant, unfurling ferns glowed in the evening light as if lit from within.
Thick, knotted roots snaked across the path, polished by generations of boots.
A warm wind murmured in the treetops, and the wood seemed to breathe.
Beyond the stream lay a black, tangled thicket where no bird sang.
No one had walked the hushed, sombre forest for years, and the trail had all but healed over.
In spring, bluebells flooded the copse, a haze of violet-blue that seemed to hover just above the ground.
The sharp, resinous scent of pine hung between the trunks.
The trees stretched away on every side, rank upon identical rank, and she had not seen another soul all day.
The glade hummed with insects, wings and the ceaseless small business of summer.
The wind stripped the last leaves from the branches and flung them, whirling, into the dark.
Ivy smothered the fallen trunk, and bright, speckled toadstools bloomed along its length.
Mist shrouded the path ahead, and every tree became a figure waiting.
